findings.title: Collision remediation instructs `cf config unset --project`, which cannot reach the stale shared copy under the design's own delete routing
findings.description: The Delete rule (line 89) states delete "mirrors write — deletes from whichever project file the key's scope maps to," meaning `cf config unset git.integration_branch --project` deletes only from `.context-forge.local.toml` (the personal file, per `CONFIG_KEYS[key].scope === 'personal'`). But the collision-semantics paragraph (line 146) tells the user that after a `migrate-personal` skip, "clearing it is a separate, explicit `cf config unset <key> --project`," and verification step 9 (line 259) makes this a success criterion: "confirm `cf check` is clean again." As specified, that unset deletes the developer's *personal* value (destroying the preference the design just said must not be overwritten) and leaves the stale shared-file copy in place, so `cf check` still reports the finding and step 9 cannot pass. The design must reconcile the two: either route `unset --project` for personal keys to delete from both project files (documented as an explicit exception, like `migrate-personal`), add a flag/targeting for the shared file, or change the remediation instruction. This is the one documented failure-recovery path that contradicts the mechanism it depends on.

findings.title: Placement of the `cf init` gitignore step relative to the `--lite` gate is unspecified, but the walkthrough requires it to run in lite mode
findings.description: The Component Structure entry says only "`init.ts` — ensures `.context-forge.local.toml` is gitignored." In the actual `init.ts`, all setup steps (guides, commands, IDE) sit inside an `if (!opts.lite)` block, and nothing in the design says whether the gitignore write runs inside or outside that gate. The verification walkthrough (steps 1–3) runs `cf init --lite` in an empty directory and then asserts `cat .gitignore` contains the line — which only holds if the step runs outside the lite gate. An implementer placing it alongside the other setup steps would break a stated success criterion. The design should say explicitly that the gitignore append runs unconditionally (before/independent of the `!opts.lite` setup block), and clarify the stated failure handling ("aborts `cf init`") given that every other failure in that region of `init.ts` is warn-and-continue, not abort.

findings.title: Line 32 claims reuse of an existing personal-ignore gitignore pattern that does not exist
findings.description: The Technical Scope bullet says the gitignore addition is "reusing the pattern already used for personal ignores," but the design's own `.gitignore` section (line 159) and a repo-wide grep of `packages/cli` and `packages/core` both confirm there is no gitignore-writing logic anywhere today. Line 159 is correct; line 32's justification is dead and should be dropped so it doesn't send an implementer looking for a nonexistent helper.

findings.title: Existing already-initialized projects get no path to gitignore coverage for the new personal file
findings.description: The gitignore write lives only in `cf init`, which matches the slice plan entry's wording ("`cf init` should ensure the personal-scope file is covered by `.gitignore`"), so this is not a plan deviation. Worth noting for the record: on a project initialized before this slice, the first `cf config set git.integration_branch ... --project` creates an un-gitignored `.context-forge.local.toml`, and neither the new `personal-config-in-shared-file` check nor anything else flags that state — the file can be committed silently until someone re-runs `cf init`. If the design wants its stated value ("prevents personal settings from being silently committed") to hold for existing projects, the natural lightweight extension is for the same `ConsistencyChecker` rule (or `cf init` re-run guidance in its message) to note the missing gitignore line; if deliberately left out, a sentence saying so would close the question.
